column6: Daniel explains the writing against Belshazzar as a weighing that finds him deficient; the commentary likewise reads loss as an account coming up light at judgment, though Daniel addresses a king's immediate downfall.

The Aramaic verdict says Belshazzar was found lacking after weighing; this gives the commentary's خسر as deficit at the scales a precise semantic analogue, while the proposed root correspondence remains unverified.
Daniel first says Belshazzar's kingdom has been numbered and brought to an end; this joins the commentary's allotted time to the closing of a judicial account.
At the heavenly court books are opened before judgment; this corresponds to the commentary's deeds present as a record when each person's account closes.
Daniel's people whose names are found written in the book are delivered at the time of distress; the commentary likewise makes a recorded status matter at the decisive day.
Daniel distinguishes the awakened dead by everlasting life or disgrace; this corresponds to the commentary's final division of good and bad, with a bodily resurrection in Daniel's setting.

column5: time for every work and judgment
column6: Qoheleth says God will judge righteous and wicked because there is a time for every matter and every work; this directly joins the commentary's allotted time, work, and judgment.

column5: every deed and hidden thing judged
column6: Qoheleth says God will bring every deed, including hidden good or evil, to judgment; the commentary similarly makes even tiny acts present at the final account.

Qoheleth asks what gain a person gets from all his toil under the sun; the commentary hears human loss beside work and passing time, though this verse questions earthly gain rather than announcing final punishment.
Qoheleth surveys his works and toil and finds no lasting gain; this sharpens the commentary's accounting sense of human loss, while its exception for good deeds gives another outcome.
Qoheleth urges doing whatever work one's hand finds because the grave has no work; the commentary likewise treats time as a deadline for deeds that later face accounting.

column5: let God weigh in just scales
column6: Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so God may know his integrity; the commentary likewise pictures scales settling a person's case by what he has done.

column5: Hebrew חקק in fixed bounds; table sound correspondence
column6: Job says human days and their limits have been prescribed and cannot be crossed; this makes concrete the commentary's appointed term within its reading of حَقّ and the day of reckoning, without equating Hebrew statute with Arabic truth.
Proverbs says the one who weighs hearts knows excuses and repays each person according to work; this combines the commentary's scales, personal deeds, and binding recompense.

column5: apparently pure ways weighed by God
column6: A person sees his ways as pure, but the Lord weighs the spirits; this probes the commentary's case of people confident their work is good before divine measurement.
Proverbs attributes just scales and weights to the Lord; this anchors the commentary's judgment-day balance in a concrete image of divine fairness.
The Lord searches the heart and repays each person according to ways and fruit of deeds; the commentary's day likewise brings each person to the consequence of his work.

God says he will judge each Israelite according to that person's ways and calls for repentance; this gives the commentary's individual work-based account a setting where conduct can still change before judgment.
The psalm says the Lord repays a person according to work; this is the same work-to-recompense relation used to explain the commentary's appointed day.

The psalm places human ranks in balances and finds them lighter than breath; the commentary likewise visualizes human loss as insufficient weight, though the psalm weighs human frailty and pretension.

column5: speak together and book of remembrance
column6: Those who fear the Lord speak to one another and a book of remembrance is written before him; this joins the surah's mutual counsel to the commentary's record of deeds.

At God's coming action people will again distinguish the righteous from the wicked and the one who serves God from one who does not; the commentary likewise ends with good and bad separated by their conduct.
The Lord names the day on which he acts and spares those he calls his own; this supplies a concrete appointed-day counterpart to the commentary's exception from loss.
Judah's sin is written with an iron stylus on the tablet of the heart; this gives a bodily image of deeds as an enduring record beside the commentary's account attached to each person.
God says the offense is written before him and that he will repay; this pairs the commentary's present record of acts with inescapable recompense.
The psalm says God sets iniquities and secret sins before him; the commentary likewise says what people did will be present rather than lost from the account.
God says he will set the wrongdoer's acts before his eyes when rebuking him; this closely matches the commentary's claim that one's own deeds confront one at judgment.
The Amorites' iniquity has not yet reached its full measure, delaying judgment; this provides an appointed accumulation of evil beside the commentary's heap of bad deeds.

The person rooted in the Lord's instruction prospers in what he does; this gives the commentary's righteous works an outcome opposed to loss, although Hebrew prosperity is not identical to Arabic صالح deeds.
Joshua is told to observe and do the law so his way will prosper; the link to the commentary is the joined action and favorable result, with only a proposed sound correspondence between roots.
Jeremiah asks why the way of the wicked prospers even though God is just; that apparent present success complicates the commentary's final separation of good works from loss.
The psalm urges waiting before the Lord while a person carrying out wicked schemes prospers; its temporary success reverses the commentary's judgment-day valuation of works.

Daniel prospers after his deliverance from the lions; this gives a narrative setting for good outcome after steadfastness beside the commentary's good work and patience, without making the roots proven cognates.
The righteous eats to satisfaction while the wicked person's belly lacks; this maps the commentary's good/bad division onto a concrete lack, though Proverbs speaks of present provision.
The psalm says seekers of the Lord lack no good thing; that absence of lack is a pointed counterpart to the commentary's exception from human loss.

Proverbs calls the adulterer lacking in sense and says he destroys himself; the commentary's loss through sinful deeds gains a specific self-destructive example, though the Hebrew lack first denotes understanding.
Deuteronomy reserves vengeance and repayment for the time when the wrongdoers' foot slips; the commentary likewise lets a fixed time mature into binding recompense.
Proverbs tells the hearer to bind loyalty and truth around the neck; the commentary's record bound to each person's neck meets a contrasting image in which truth is what one chooses to carry.

column5: speak truth to neighbor and judge justly
column6: Zechariah joins truthful speech to one's neighbor with judgments of truth and peace at the gates; this gives the surah's mutual counsel in truth a communal judicial setting.
Paul says God has fixed a day to judge the world in righteousness; this directly corresponds to the commentary's named day on which the claim of justice becomes binding.
The Son of Man comes in glory and repays each person according to conduct; the commentary likewise brings everyone to an appointed day and settles the account by works.
Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the world while forfeiting one's life; this gives the commentary's human loss a pointed accounting comparison.
Paul says God repays each person according to works; this precisely matches the commentary's explanation that the day assigns each human a consequence by work.
Paul assigns eternal life to those who persist in doing good; this combines the commentary's good deeds, patient endurance, and exception from loss.
Paul contrasts those who reject truth and follow wrongdoing with the patient doers of good, assigning wrath; this connects the commentary's communicated truth and bad works to its final division.
All must appear before Christ's judgment seat and receive what is due for deeds, good or bad; this is a close counterpart to the commentary's two classes of work and inescapable accounting.
The dead stand before the throne while books are opened and are judged by what their works record; this joins the commentary's present deeds to its individual ledger and final tribunal.
Death and Hades yield the dead, who are judged individually according to deeds; the commentary likewise insists each person meets the consequence of his own work.
The coming speaker brings recompense to repay everyone for what each has done; this links the commentary's approaching appointed day to personal reward.
The Son of Man gathers the nations and separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats; this supplies a scene for the commentary's final sorting of good from bad.
The welcomed people fed the hungry and gave drink to the thirsty; the commentary's righteous deeds gain small, tangible instances used in the final verdict.

column5: act for the least counted for the king
column6: The king says deeds done for one of the least of his family were done for him; this makes the commentary's minute good deed unexpectedly weighty at final judgment.
The rejected are sent to eternal fire after the separation; this connects the commentary's inverted patience, doing the works of fire's people, to a final destination.
The passage concludes with punishment for one group and life for the righteous; this matches the commentary's decisive division after the accounting.
Jesus describes angels separating evil people from righteous at the end of the age; this is a direct counterpart to the commentary's end-time distinction between bad and good.
Anyone absent from the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire; this joins the commentary's record and the fire-bound consequence of evil work.

column5: spur one another to good works
column6: The community is to consider how to provoke one another to love and good works; this parallels the surah's mutual counsel and righteous action as a collective practice.
Believers are to encourage one another increasingly as they see the Day approaching; this meets both the surah's reciprocal exhortation and the commentary's deadline.

column5: exhort one another while today lasts
column6: The community is told to exhort one another daily while it is called Today, lest sin harden them; this makes mutual counsel a time-limited defense against losing one's way.
The saints' endurance is described as keeping God's commands and faith in Jesus; this places patience, faith, and action together beside the surah's exception.
God is just and will not forget the work and love shown in service; this complements the commentary's claim that deeds remain present for a just account.
The community is urged to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience; this gives the surah's faith and endurance an explicit outcome.
Paul says a person reaps what he sows; this is another precise work-to-consequence formula for the commentary's day of settlement.
Paul separates sowing to flesh from sowing to Spirit, with corruption or eternal life as outcomes; this parallels the commentary's good/bad work distinction and loss.

column5: do good patiently until due season
column6: Paul urges not wearying in doing good because harvest comes at the right time if one does not give up; this joins the commentary's good deeds, patience, and appointed term.
The faithful are urged to abound in the Lord's work because their labor is not vain; this directly reverses the surah's general human loss through faithful action.
Paul says a burned work brings loss while its worker may still be saved through fire; this complicates the commentary's alignment of deficient works, personal loss, and fire.
The Day exposes each person's work and fire tests its quality; this is a concrete counterpart to deeds becoming present and differentiated at judgment.
Many appeal to prophecy, exorcism, and mighty works done in Jesus' name on that day; this mirrors the commentary's people who think their efforts good before judgment.
Jesus rejects those claimants as workers of lawlessness; the commentary likewise says apparent good effort can prove valueless when the actual work is judged.
Jesus says people will give account on judgment day even for careless speech; this gives the commentary's tiny measured deed a speech-sized counterpart.
Jesus says a cup of water given to his people will not lose its reward; this answers the commentary's claim that even the smallest good is seen in the account.

column5: hidden matters disclosed and praise allotted
column6: At the Lord's coming, hidden things and heart motives are brought to light before praise is assigned; this parallels the commentary's deeds made present, while adding intent to visible work.
Paul says a hard heart stores up wrath for the day of righteous judgment; this meets the commentary's accumulated evil and appointed day.
Jesus tells his opponents to fill up the measure of their ancestors; this makes moral evil accumulate toward judgment like the commentary's bad things piled one on another.
The corrosion of hoarded riches testifies against the rich, who have stored treasure in the last days; the commentary's bad accumulation likewise becomes evidence at the final reckoning.
God tells the rich planner that his life is required that night and asks who will own his stores; this makes the commentary's deadline and lost balance concrete in an unexpected accounting.
Peter distinguishes endurance under punishment for sin from endurance when one does good and suffers; this clarifies the commentary's reversal of patience into work meriting fire.
The Lord's revelation in fire brings punishment upon those who disobey the gospel; this connects the commentary's fire-bound work to a judicial rather than merely physical fire.
The psalm asks to number our days so that wisdom may follow; this supports the commentary's allotted-time reading, though it teaches present wisdom rather than describing final scales.
Job imagines his transgression sealed in a bag before God; this offers another personal record of wrong beside the commentary's deeds kept for later confrontation.
God says the one who sins against him will be erased from his book; this reverses the commentary's image of acts attached to the person while keeping the same individual-account logic.

column5: remember deeds and do not blot them
column6: Nehemiah asks God not to wipe out his deeds done for the temple; the commentary's good works present at judgment have a concrete prayer for preserved memory.

Isaiah condemns those who decree unjust decrees; this sets an unjust human use of prescribed law against the commentary's binding just recompense on the day, without treating Hebrew lawmaking as Arabic truth.
Proverbs tells the hearer to tie parental teaching around the neck; beside the commentary's deed record attached there, this shows a life-guiding text voluntarily carried before judgment.
The one who gives to the poor will not lack, while ignoring them brings curses; this gives the commentary's good-deed exception from loss a material example.

The psalmist understands the prosperous wicked only after entering God's sanctuary and considering their end; this interprets the commentary's loss as an eventual outcome beyond apparent present success.
Job says humans are born to trouble; this shares the commentary's universal human condition but locates it in earthly toil rather than necessarily in punishment for misdeeds.
The Mishnah says all inhabitants of the world pass before God for judgment at the new year; this interprets the commentary's every-person account through a recurring Jewish liturgical day.
The Talmud speaks of books opened for the righteous, wicked, and intermediate at the new year; this gives the commentary's present deeds and good/bad division a specific Jewish record tradition.

The discussion urges a person to imagine oneself and the world balanced between merit and liability so one deed can tip the outcome; this interprets the commentary's minute weighed acts as morally consequential.
Avot describes an open ledger, a writing hand, collectors, and a true judgment of all actions; this supplies a detailed account metaphor for the commentary's closing of each person's record.
Avot says one commandment gains an advocate and one transgression an accuser; this personifies the commentary's good and bad acts standing ready when judged.

column5: give an account to the King
column6: Avot says a person will eventually give a reckoning before the King of kings; this parallels the commentary's inevitable personal settlement after one's allotted life.
Avot urges calculating a commandment's loss against its reward and a sin's gain against its loss; this gives the commentary's profit-and-deficit language an explicit moral ledger tradition.
Hebrews says human death is appointed once, followed by judgment; this gives the commentary's allotted time and settling day a succinct sequence.

column5: world kept for judgment by fire
column6: The present world is kept for the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly by fire; this connects the commentary's deadline to the fire-bound result of bad works.

column5: patience until coming as farmer waits
column6: James tells believers to wait patiently for the Lord's coming like a farmer awaiting the crop; this gives the surah's patience and the commentary's appointed end a seasonal image.
The warning against grumbling says the Judge is standing at the doors; this ties communal conduct while waiting to an imminent accounting.
Believers are instructed to speak truth with neighbors because they belong to one another; this gives the surah's reciprocal counsel in truth a communal relation.

column5: impressive charity without love gains nothing
column6: Even giving away all possessions gains nothing without love; this illuminates the commentary's apparently good efforts that prove valueless when judged by their real character.
Jesus says the humble tax collector, rather than the self-assured Pharisee, goes home justified; this offers a concrete reversal of people who suppose their own work good.
Jesus warns that righteousness performed to be seen by others receives no reward from the Father; this specifies why work that looks good might fail the commentary's account.

column5: work of faith and patient hope
column6: Paul remembers the community's work of faith and endurance of hope; this places action, faith, and patience together as the surah's exception does.
God considers it just to repay affliction to those who afflict believers; this concretizes the commentary's binding recompense as reversal for injurious work.

column5: Hebrew צבר; table sound correspondence; piled wealth
column6: Job says a wicked person may heap up silver; the next verse transfers what he prepared to the righteous, making material accumulation and final loss an indirect counterpart to the commentary's piled evil. The Hebrew heaping sense is distinct from Arabic patience.

column5: wicked's stores enjoyed by just people
column6: Job says the just will wear what the wicked prepared; this indirectly reverses the commentary's piled bad deeds into an earthly redistribution rather than an end-time scale.

column5: Hebrew צבר; table sound correspondence; heaped goods
column6: The psalm says a person heaps things without knowing who will gather them; this provides a time-limited loss for amassed goods, only an indirect parallel to the commentary's heap of bad works. The Hebrew heaping sense is distinct from Arabic patience.
Isaiah tells the righteous they will eat the fruit of their deeds; this is a direct good-work counterpart to the commentary's final division and recompense.
The next verse says the wicked will receive what their own hands have done; it supplies the adverse half of the commentary's work-by-work settlement.
Hosea says the people forget that God remembers their evil, while their deeds now surround them and stand before him; this closely matches the commentary's deeds found present at the account.
Elihu says God repays a person for work and causes each to find the consequence of a way; this states the commentary's personal work-to-recompense formula in another setting.

column5: eyes on all ways and deeds
column6: Jeremiah praises God's eyes upon all human ways so as to give each according to conduct and the fruit of deeds; this joins the commentary's complete record to individual repayment.

Ezekiel denies that child or parent bears the other's guilt and assigns each one's righteousness or wickedness to that person; this specifies the commentary's every-person account as individually owned.

Ezekiel says a turning sinner's former transgressions will not be remembered when he lives by righteousness; this qualifies the commentary's image of every past deed remaining present in the final record.

The psalm's qualified guest walks blamelessly, does righteousness, and speaks truth in the heart; this combines good action and truth as the surah's exception does, with access to God's dwelling as its outcome.

column5: books of sins and stored righteousness
column6: The apocalypse places written sins beside treasuries of righteous deeds when judgment arrives; this develops the commentary's present records and divided good and bad acts into two kinds of stored evidence.

The apocalyptic description says works follow, reward appears, good deeds awaken, and wicked deeds do not sleep; this gives the commentary's acts found present at judgment a vivid independent formulation.

column5: recompense at death according to conduct
column6: Sirach says it is easy for the Lord to repay a person at death according to that person's ways; this joins the commentary's allotted term and binding individual recompense.
A voice says those who die in the Lord rest from labors and their works follow them; this closely meets the commentary's time limit, enduring good works, and deeds present afterward.

column5: doers of good and evil rise differently
column6: Jesus says those who have done good rise to life and those who have done evil to judgment; this makes the commentary's good and bad deeds decisive at the final separation.
James says faith by itself is dead if it has no works; this gives the surah's pairing of belief and righteous deeds a specific consequence when action is absent.
Jesus tells threatened disciples they will gain their lives through endurance; this sets patient perseverance directly opposite the commentary's human loss.

column5: endure to end and be saved
column6: The hated disciple who endures to the end will be saved; this joins the surah's patience to the commentary's deadline and exception from loss.
The risen speaker tells Sardis that its works have not been found complete before God; this is a precise counterpart to the commentary's apparently good work that fails the final assessment.

column5: impartial judgment of each one's work
column6: Peter says the Father judges impartially according to each person's work and tells believers to conduct themselves in reverent fear during their time away; this joins personal deeds, just measurement, and a limited present term.
Hebrews says endurance is needed so that, after doing God's will, the hearers may receive the promise; this links good action and patience to a future recompense.
Jesus adds that one's own words will justify or condemn; this gives the commentary's exact accounting an explicit verdict for the small speech acts named in the preceding verse.
Jesus says entry into the kingdom belongs to one doing his Father's will, which explains why the impressive acts claimed in the following verse can still fail the commentary's good-work test.
The rejected did not feed the hungry or give drink to the thirsty; this supplies the negative half of the commentary's smallest deed carrying weight at the division.
The speaker says he searches mind and heart and will give each person according to works; this adds the inward quality of deeds to the commentary's personal final account.
Daniel's third explanation says Belshazzar's kingdom is divided and given away; it specifies what is lost when the weighed account in the preceding verse proves deficient.

Proverbs contrasts gain from labor with need arising from mere talk, using the table's Hebrew lack root; this is a present-life analogue to the commentary's work and loss account, not an end-time verdict.

column5: Hebrew חקק in decree; table sound correspondence
column6: Zephaniah urges action before the decree takes effect and before the Lord's angry day arrives; this places a prescribed term beside the commentary's appointed judgment day, while the root link remains unverified.

After the fruitful righteous person, the psalm depicts wicked people as chaff driven away by wind; this supplies a contrasting failure of substance beside the commentary's separated losers, without asserting a literal scale.

The apocalyptic court opens books of the living before the divine presence; this develops the commentary's record-and-day scene, though the books concern those counted as living rather than a list of every act.
Ephesians explicitly denies that salvation arises from works, complicating a reading of the commentary's good deeds as the basis of rescue from loss.
The next verse says believers are made for good works prepared for them to walk in; this preserves good action alongside the preceding grace claim and the surah's believing doers.
Paul says faith works through love; this gives the surah's paired belief and action a concrete communal form rather than treating faith as mere assent.
Peter says the Lord's apparent delay expresses patience so people may repent; this gives the commentary's appointed day a different role for patience, allowing change before the account closes.
The rejected ask when they failed to serve the king in his needs; their surprise is a concrete instance of the commentary's people who misjudge the worth of their own conduct.
The Laodiceans claim to need nothing but are called poor and exposed; this supplies the commentary's self-mistaken assessment with a striking deficit image.
Jesus says greater trust brings a greater demand; this is a specific proportional-account rule beside the commentary's precise weighing of each person's acts.
Paul promises relief to the afflicted when the Lord is revealed; this completes the reversal of affliction and repayment in the surrounding judgment passage and the commentary's righteous exception.

Augustine discusses the books opened at the last judgment as a disclosure of what people have done, possibly through divine recall rather than physical ledgers; this changes how the commentary's visible account can be imagined.

column5: qere לו; deeds measured by God
column6: In Hannah's song the traditional qere makes God the one by whom deeds are measured, closely matching the commentary's scales for human action; WLC's written ketiv ולא differs, so this connection depends on the named reading.

column5: WLC ketiv ולא versus qere לו
column6: The written ketiv can be read as denying that deeds are measured, unlike the commentary's scales; the familiar qere gives the opposite sense, so the reversal is textually uncertain and should be checked against the WLC stream.

A scene in this recension appears to bring a soul's merits and sins into a heavenly weighing, close to the commentary's personal balance; the chapter placement and the roles of the heavenly figures are uncertain from memory.
